c.tagline: Andalusian city of the Mezquita, patio courtyards, and three cultures woven in stone.

taxi.fareNote: Uber does not operate in Córdoba; Cabify and licensed metered white taxis are the options.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in the centre and around the bus terminal; caution at night

hood_desc: Córdoba's iconic UNESCO old quarter of whitewashed lanes and flower-filled courtyards wrapped around the Mezquita-Catedral; the most atmospheric — and most photographed — place to stay, with landmarks at every turn.
The lively commercial heart around Plaza de las Tendillas, full of shops, tapas bars and tabernas; a convenient, well-connected base a short walk from the monuments.
The Alcázar Viejo neighborhood famous for its award-winning private patios and the May Patios Festival; a quieter, quintessentially Cordoban corner beside the Alcázar and the old city walls.
The historic eastern old town around the arcaded Plaza de la Corredera, with lively local markets, taverns and a less touristy, more authentic buzz after dark.
The modern district around the AVE high-speed station and the Vial Norte, with contemporary hotels and easy transport; practical and affordable, a 15-minute walk or quick bus from the old town.
lodging: Las Casas de la Judería de Córdoba

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: City buses generally run from about 6:30 AM to 11:00 PM, with a limited late-night line on weekends; there is no metro or tram.
transit.note: Córdoba's compact historic core is best explored on foot; public transport is the AUCORSA city bus network, supplemented by taxis. There is no metro or tram.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash (single ~€1.30) or tap the rechargeable Tarjeta de Transporte / bank card; day and multi-trip cards offer discounts.

air: Nearest: Seville Airport (SVQ, ~130 km) or Málaga Airport (AGP, ~165 km)
bus: Córdoba bus station (intercity ALSA coaches, next to the train station)
train: Córdoba railway station (AVE high-speed to Madrid, Seville & Málaga; Renfe long-distance and Media Distancia)

airport.name: Seville Airport (SVQ) — nearest with scheduled flights (~130 km); Córdoba's own airport has no regular commercial service

transit.m: Airport bus EA to Sevilla-Santa Justa, then Renfe/AVE train to Córdoba (~1.5 hr total)
Direct taxi/transfer from Seville Airport to Córdoba (~1 hr 20 min)

tip.r: Service is included; locals typically round up or leave small change, or 5-10% for good restaurant service.

food.name: Salmorejo cordobés
food.desc: Córdoba's own thick, chilled tomato and bread cream, far denser than gazpacho, finished with chopped jamón and hard-boiled egg.

places.name: Bodegas Campos
places.note: Landmark bodega since 1908 with barrel-lined rooms and a benchmark salmorejo.

places.name: Taberna Salinas
places.note: Working since 1879; classic Córdoban tapas at old-fashioned prices.

places.name: Casa Pepe de la Judería
places.note: Andalusian standards done well, with a roof terrace facing the cathedral-mosque.

food.name: Rabo de toro
food.desc: Oxtail braised for hours in Montilla wine until it slides off the bone, usually served with fried potatoes; the city's defining meat dish.

places.name: La Viuda
places.note: Named best rabo de toro in Córdoba for 2025 by the local oxtail brotherhood.

places.name: Casa Pepe de la Judería
places.note: Slow-cooked oxtail is the house classic; book ahead for the terrace.

places.name: El Churrasco
places.note: Long-running grill house also strong on charcoal-cooked Iberian pork.

food.name: Flamenquín cordobés
food.desc: A roll of pork loin wrapped around jamón serrano, breaded and deep fried; born in Córdoba province and eaten as a tapa or a full plate.

places.name: Taberna San Miguel El Pisto
places.note: Tiled 1880s tavern that locals treat as the standard for Córdoban tapas.

places.name: Sociedad de Plateros María Auxiliadora
places.note: Historic silversmiths' guild tavern with a courtyard and honest prices.

places.name: Bodegas Mezquita
places.note: Reliable tapas kitchen with several branches and a shop of local produce.

food.name: Berenjenas con miel de caña
food.desc: Batons of aubergine fried light and crisp then drizzled with dark sugarcane molasses; the sweet-salty tapa everyone in Córdoba orders first.

places.name: Bodegas Mezquita
places.note: Consistently good version, served in tapa or sharing size.

places.name: Taberna La Montillana
places.note: Modern Córdoban cooking with a strong local wine list; popular with locals.

places.name: Casa Mazal
places.note: Sephardic-leaning kitchen in the Jewish quarter with a pretty patio.

food.name: Mazamorra cordobesa
food.desc: The white ancestor of salmorejo, made from almonds, bread, garlic and oil, chilled and topped with apple or cod; older than tomatoes in Spain.

places.name: Taberna La Montillana
places.note: Keeps the almond mazamorra on alongside salmorejo so you can compare the two.

places.name: Bodegas Campos
places.note: Traditional recipes served in a warren of historic dining rooms.

places.name: Casa Rubio
places.note: Tapas bar beside the old city wall, good for a first round of cold soups.

food.name: Tortilla de patatas and taberna tapas
food.desc: Córdoba's tabernas run on thick, barely set potato omelette, jamón, oxtail croquettes and salt cod, ordered a plate at a time with wine.

places.name: Bar Santos
places.note: Famous for a towering tortilla eaten on the steps facing the Mezquita wall.

places.name: Taberna Salinas
places.note: Patio tavern from 1879 where the tapas list has barely changed in decades.

places.name: Sociedad de Plateros María Auxiliadora
places.note: Big, unfussy plates and jugs of Montilla in a courtyard setting.

food.name: Montilla-Moriles fino
food.desc: Bone-dry, sherry-like white from the hills south of the city, aged under flor and poured cold from the barrel with every tapa.

places.name: Taberna San Miguel El Pisto
places.note: Fino straight from the cask in a tavern lined with bullfighting tiles.

places.name: Bodegas Campos
places.note: Deep Montilla-Moriles list and its own house-labelled barrels.

places.name: Taberna Salinas
places.note: The everyday local ritual: a chilled fino and a plate of something fried.

food.name: Pedro Ximénez sweet wine
food.desc: Sun-dried Pedro Ximénez grapes make a near-black, raisin-sweet dessert wine from the same Montilla-Moriles hills; often poured over ice cream.

places.name: Bodegas Mezquita
places.note: Easy place to taste PX by the glass and buy a bottle in the attached shop.

places.name: Bodegas Campos
places.note: Older PX bottlings available by the glass to close a long lunch.

places.name: Casa Pepe de la Judería
places.note: Serves PX with dessert on the terrace above the Jewish quarter rooftops.

landmarks: Mezquita-Catedral (Mosque-Cathedral)
A forest of 850 candy-striped arches from the great Umayyad mosque encloses a Renaissance cathedral, creating Spain's most breathtaking and singular monument.
Puente Romano (Roman Bridge)
Sixteen honey-coloured arches have spanned the Guadalquivir since Augustus, framing the Mezquita in Córdoba's classic floodlit evening panorama.
Alcázar de los Reyes Cristianos
The fortress-palace of the Catholic Monarchs pairs Mudéjar courtyards and Roman mosaics with terraced gardens of fountains, ponds and orange trees.
Judería and Calleja de las Flores
Córdoba's whitewashed medieval Jewish quarter tangles into flower-hung lanes, none more famous than this geranium-lined alley framing the cathedral tower.
Medina Azahara
The ruined 10th-century palace-city of Caliph Abd al-Rahman III, a UNESCO site outside town, evokes the dazzling apex of Umayyad Córdoba.
Palacio de Viana
An aristocratic mansion celebrated for twelve linked patios, each a distinct garden of citrus, jasmine and azulejos, the essence of Córdoba's courtyard culture.
Sinagoga de Córdoba
One of Spain's only three surviving medieval synagogues, this intimate 1315 Mudéjar prayer hall bears delicate stucco and Hebrew inscriptions.
Torre de la Calahorra
The fortified Moorish gate-tower across the Roman Bridge houses a museum on Al-Andalus and rewards climbers with river-and-Mezquita views.
Plaza de la Corredera
Andalusia's only grand Castilian-style square, a 17th-century arcaded rectangle once used for bullfights, now lined with tapas terraces and market stalls.
Templo Romano
Eleven soaring reconstructed Corinthian columns beside city hall mark the podium of a first-century Roman temple, dramatic when illuminated at night.

train.note: No international trains. Córdoba is a key junction on Spain's high-speed network: AVE trains reach Madrid in about 1h45, Seville in 45 minutes and Málaga in under an hour, with Ouigo and Iryo also on the Madrid route. The station is a 20-minute walk north of the Mezquita. Booking opens around 60 days ahead and the Andalusian routes are busy in spring.

bus.note: The bus station is opposite the railway station. ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en) runs to Granada, Seville, Málaga and Madrid, though the AVE is much faster on most of those. International coaches generally route through Madrid or Seville.

ferry.note: Córdoba is inland on the Guadalquivir, which is no longer navigable this far upstream, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Priego de Córdoba
half.blurb: Baroque hill town known for its whitewashed old quarter, ornate churches, and a dramatic balcony overlooking the Subbética countryside.

half.name: Zuheros
half.blurb: Whitewashed village clinging to a cliff beneath a Moorish castle, with a prehistoric cave nearby in the Sierra Subbética.

half.name: Seville
half.blurb: Andalusian capital with a Gothic cathedral, the Real Alcázar palace, and the Plaza de España, reachable by fast train.

full.name: Granada
full.blurb: Home to the Alhambra palace-fortress and the Albaicín's winding Moorish quarter, set below the Sierra Nevada mountains.
